title: Jijuyu Zanmai, Escape This Crazy Life of Tears
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: The talk's main teaching is that even in moments of confusion or uncertainty, one can discover profound truths through practice and engagement with Buddhist rituals and ceremonies. By truly embodying these practices, such as Zazen and Zuisei ceremonies, one can experience a magical transformation and come to appreciate the deeper meaning behind them. This involves not just following external forms, but also cultivating mindfulness, compassion, and respect for others, ultimately leading to personal growth and spiritual development.

*When even for a moment you sit upright in Samadhi, in Zazen in other words, expressing the Buddha Mudra in the three activities, the whole world of phenomena becomes the Buddha Mudra, and the entire sky turns into enlightenment.
Accordingly, all Buddha Tathagatas increased Dharma bliss, the original source, and renewed their magnificence in the awakening of the way.

Furthermore, all beings in the world of phenomena in the ten directions and the six paths, including the three lower paths, at once, all of a sudden at once obtain pure body and mind, realize the state of great emancipation, and manifest the original face.

At this moment, this moment, when you're sitting Zazen, all things actualize true awakening, myriad objects partake of the Buddha body, and sitting upright, a glorious one under the Bodhi tree, you immediately leap beyond the boundary of awakening.
Then, you turn the unsurpassedly great Dharma wheel, and expound the profound wisdom, ultimate and unconditioned.*
That's the opening passage of Jijuyu Zanmai.
So this is very astounding, right?
If you read this and you really believe what he's saying here, it's quite astounding.
At first it seems like a lot of religious jargon, hopelessly in the clouds.

I mean, we thought it was just me and you, regular people in 21st century Bellingham, Washington, in the United States of America, sitting Zazen on our little black cushions that we got from the Dharma store.
And then we read all this.
And he's saying, actually, no, that's not what is happening.
When you're sitting in Zazen, what you think is going on has really nothing to do with what in fact is going on.

What in fact is going on is that, as soon as you sit down, Buddha is appearing in your body and your breath, and in that moment of your intention to sit Zazen and doing it, you are actually, literally, in fact, Buddha.
You just sit down and kaboom, you are already Buddha in the exact moment of awakening under the Bodhi tree.
That's what he's just said there.
Not only are you a Buddha, but you are the Buddha in that moment.
So he's saying Zazen is not meditation practice.
He says this literally in Fukanzazengi.
He says Zazen is not meditation practice.
In Fukanzazengi, he says Zazen is the Dharma gate of repose and bliss, not meditation.
And here he says Zazen is not meditation.
He doesn't say that literally.
But he says what Zazen is: the Buddha Mudra, the Buddha Mudra using your body and mind and breath to express itself.
And not only that, but in that moment, everything is expressive of the Buddha Mudra because of your sitting in Zazen.
What this amounts to is that sitting in Zazen is a kind of religious ritual.
You are partaking in a kind of magical transformation.
And honestly, I don't think this is a fantasy or an exaggeration.
I believe Dogen completely.
It really is true.

To sit in Zazen is to sit inside the world of the Lotus Sutra, with its miraculous Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and its unbelievable happenings, with its glorious vision, especially its glorious vision that all existing things are really and truly equally Buddha right now, including the suffering and the catastrophe.
That's what Dogen is saying in the passage.
He's saying that your Zazen is for the purpose of manifesting this and revealing it to be so, even though whether or not you sit in Zazen, it's so anyway.

It's not poetry per se.
It's a poetic diary of a pilgrimage trip that a number of us took to Japan for the purpose of performing a ritual known as Zuisei.
Zuisei is a ritual that is performed by Soto Zen Buddhist priests after they complete their Dharma transmission ceremonies.
You do your Dharma transmission ceremonies, usually in your home temple, and then you perform Zuisei twice.
Zuisei has two ceremonies, one at Eiheiji and one at Sojiji, the two big headquarters monasteries of Soto Zen.
When I received Shiho in 2000, I mean, not 2000, 1988, I didn't want to do that, because I thought, I'm not Japanese, and why should I go all the way to Japan and pay a lot of money?
Incidentally, it costs a lot of money to do these ceremonies.

So, long story short, we started the Soto Zen Buddhist Association and we created a ceremony, and now Soto Zen Buddhist priests who complete Shiho do a version of the Zuisei ceremony in America.
But in 2010, some how many, 30 years later, I decided, let's go to Japan, and for the fun of it I'll do the Zuisei ceremony now, 30 years later.
It's kind of funny, because in Japan priests who receive Shiho are usually young, right?
You receive Shiho at the beginning of your career.
So all the people who do Zuisei are usually young men.

The Japanese did not know what to think about this.
It's totally odd in every way.
But anyway, we did it, because it was fun to do and interesting, and we needed a good excuse, an organizing principle for our trip.
So *Escape This Crazy Life of Tears* is a diary in poetic form that I wrote along the way of the trip and then edited into a text, and it was published by a poetry press in Hawaii.
I forget what year it was published, 2014, 2014.

Here we are in Japan, right?
We're wearing the same robes that the Japanese wear.

And they see the modern world ignoring all this, right?

My wife Cathy, who some of you know is also a Zen Buddhist priest and now doing quite a bit of Zen teaching and leading, always says to everybody, when she talks about ritual, "This is not a performance."

What she means by that is, let's not get caught in the stupid trap that a lot of Zen centers get caught in, of being very uptight and perfectionistic about the rituals, as if the ritual was a kind of performance, and if you made a mistake you would be criticized, and if you did it right you would get a big pat on the back, as if you had just done a piano recital and it was a smash hit.

What I mean by that is, just like an actor who disappears into a role, so that the role in the moment that she's performing it is completely real, more real in that moment than her everyday personality.
